The Short-tailed swift (Chaetura brachyura) is a small neotropical apodid that exhibits a set of life-history traits shaped by its highly aerial lifestyle. Females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] with a typical clutch size ranging from 3 to 4 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size ranging from 3 to 4 eggs], though clutches of up to 7 eggs have been documented occasionally. The incubation period for this species, recorded under the thermal conditions of the incubating nest at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts between 17 and 18 days [ab = between 17 and 18 days]. Hatchlings emerge at a very modest neonatal wet weight of 1.6 grams [Wwb = 1.6 grams], a value that reflects the altricial state typical of swift neonates and places substantial energetic demands on both parents during the subsequent nestling period.

The developmental trajectory of the altricial nestling involves a fairly rapid mass gain such that fledgling independence is achieved well before the onset of the first breeding season. Under the parental brooding temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time from hatching to first flight, a period known as the fledging interval, lasts an average of 36 days [tx = 36 days]. This relatively extended nestling phase, compared to some other small insectivorous birds, is thought to correlate with the species' need to attain sufficient wing-loading ratios for sustained high-speed flight immediately post-departure. Once the fledgling leaves the nest, it continues to receive parental provisioning for a short period before becoming fully independent.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs relatively late for a bird of its body size. Data extrapolated from related apodids suggest that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 108 days after hatching [tp = 108 days after hatching] when maintained at a body temperature of approximately 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This developmental pace implies that juveniles hatched early in the season may attain reproductive maturity before the end of their first calendar year, but are unlikely to breed until the following reproductive season. The attainment of the maximum recorded adult body mass, a key morphological marker of adulthood, occurs gradually as the subadult bird continues to refine its foraging skills and accumulate the necessary flight musculature.

In terms of body size, adult females reach a maximum body mass of 20 grams [Wwi = 20 grams], a relatively light weight that is consistent with the streamlined, high-aspect-ratio wing morphology required for efficient aerial insectivory. The first successful breeding event typically occurs at one year of age (one year since birth) [tR = one year since birth], a timing that is based on comparative data from the congeneric Common swift (Apus apus) and takes into account the constraints imposed by the species' annual single-clutch strategy at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This deferred reproduction, relative to the time at puberty, suggests that young adults may require an extended period to acquire the necessary flight efficiency and foraging territories to successfully provision a brood.

Longevity data for the Short-tailed swift are not abundant, but the maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at 16 years [am = 16 years] under typical environmental temperatures of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] for active individuals. This relatively long lifespan, considering its small body mass, aligns with a slow-paced life-history strategy where annual adult survival is prioritized over high annual fecundity. The maximum reproductive rate, calculated from a single annual clutch of 3 to 4 eggs, translates to an annual output of 3 to 4 offspring per female per year [Ri = 3 to 4 offspring per female per year], a modest figure that underscores the species' reliance on high juvenile survival and extended breeding tenure rather than large clutch sizes to maintain stable population numbers.
